questions.question: Which one of the following species could be analysed using AAS?
questions.answer: Atomic absorption spectroscopy measures the absorption of light by free metal atoms, so it is used to analyse metal ions such as $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ (A). Sulfide, sulfur dioxide and sulfate are non-metal species.

questions.question:
The forward reaction in the equilibrium shown below is endothermic.

$$\text{OCl}^-(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{HOCl}(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq)$$

Which change increases the concentration of hypochlorous acid ($\text{HOCl}$)?
questions.answer: Adding $\text{NaOCl}$ increases $[\text{OCl}^-]$, so by Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts right and $[\text{HOCl}]$ increases (B). Water is a pure liquid so adding it does not shift the position in favour of $\text{HOCl}$; increasing the pH adds $\text{OH}^-$, shifting the equilibrium left; lowering the temperature favours the exothermic (reverse) direction.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about acid-base indicators. Acid-base indicators

(i) are weak acids or bases.
(ii) are strong acids that change colour as the concentration of hydrogen ions changes.
(iii) must not react with the reactants or products in a titration.
(iv) must be used in large volumes for the best results.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.answer: Indicators are weak acids (or bases), $\text{HIn} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{In}^-$, whose two forms have different colours, so (i) is correct and (ii) is wrong. An indicator works precisely by reacting (gaining/losing a proton) with the titrant near the end point, so (iii) is wrong, and only a few drops are used because the indicator itself consumes some titrant, so (iv) is wrong. Answer: A.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs of compounds will form a precipitate when $0.1\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ solutions of each are mixed?
questions.answer: Hydroxides of transition metals are insoluble: $\text{Cu}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{Cu(OH)}_2(s)$, a blue precipitate (D). All nitrates, potassium salts, $\text{CuSO}_4$ and $\text{CaBr}_2$ are soluble.

questions.question: How many isomers are there for a molecule with the formula $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{Cl}_2$?
questions.answer: The structural (position) isomers are 1,1-dichloropropane, 1,2-dichloropropane, 1,3-dichloropropane and 2,2-dichloropropane: 4 isomers (B).

questions.question:
Interactions between lipid and solvent molecules can result in the formation of micelles and inverse micelles as shown in the diagrams below.

Which alternative below shows the correct polarity of a solvent which would form each type of micelle?
questions.answer: In a micelle the hydrophilic heads face outwards into the solvent, so the solvent is polar (e.g. water). In an inverse micelle the hydrophobic tails face outwards, so the solvent is non-polar (B).

questions.question: Which statement relates most to NMR spectroscopy?
options: Valence electrons in metal atoms are excited, moving to a higher energy level.
The mass of a charged particle will determine its trajectory in a magnetic field.
Bonds in a molecule can absorb energy, which results in them stretching.
Protons are excited and move to a higher energy spin state.
questions.answer: NMR detects nuclei (e.g. protons) in a magnetic field absorbing radio waves and flipping to a higher-energy spin state (D). A describes AAS, B mass spectrometry and C infrared spectroscopy.

questions.question:
For the equilibrium

$$2\text{ICl}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{I}_2(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g)$$

the numerical value of the equilibrium constant $K$ is $4.8 \times 10^{-6}$ at 25°C. Which of the following statements is true at 25°C at equilibrium?
options: There will be much less $\text{I}_2$ and $\text{Cl}_2$ than $\text{ICl}$.
There will be twice as much $\text{ICl}$ as $\text{I}_2$ present.
The pressure of each gas, $\text{I}_2$, $\text{Cl}_2$ and $\text{ICl}$, will all be the same.
There will be much more $\text{I}_2$ and $\text{Cl}_2$ than $\text{ICl}$.
questions.answer: $K = \dfrac{[\text{I}_2][\text{Cl}_2]}{[\text{ICl}]^2}$ is very small, so the equilibrium lies far to the left: there is much less $\text{I}_2$ and $\text{Cl}_2$ than $\text{ICl}$ (A).

questions.question: Which of the following is true for a system at equilibrium?
options: The number of collisions per unit time between reactants is equal to the number of collisions per unit time between products.
The product of the concentrations of the reactants is equal to the product of the concentrations of the products.
Reactants are reacting to form products at the same rate as products are reacting to form reactants.
All concentrations of reactants and products are equal.
questions.answer: Dynamic equilibrium means the forward and reverse reaction rates are equal (C), so concentrations stay constant; they are not necessarily equal to each other.

questions.question: The pH of pure water at 50°C ($K_w = 5.5 \times 10^{-14}$) is:
questions.answer: In pure water $[\text{H}^+] = [\text{OH}^-]$, so $[\text{H}^+] = \sqrt{5.5 \times 10^{-14}} = 2.35 \times 10^{-7}$ M and $\text{pH} = -\log_{10}(2.35 \times 10^{-7}) = 6.63$ (A). The water is still neutral because $[\text{H}^+] = [\text{OH}^-]$.

questions.question:
The graph below refers to the following gaseous reaction.

$$a\text{A}(g) + b\text{B}(g) \rightleftharpoons c\text{C}(g) + d\text{D}(g)$$

The effect of increasing pressure and temperature on the equilibrium yield of the products is shown in the graph. Which of the following alternatives regarding the chemical system is consistent with the data?
questions.answer: Yield increases with pressure, so the forward reaction produces fewer moles of gas: $a + b > c + d$. Yield decreases as temperature increases, so the forward reaction is exothermic, $\Delta H < 0$. Answer: C.

questions.question: Iodine monochloride ($\text{ICl}$) reacts with carbon-carbon double bonds via an addition reaction (one $\text{ICl}$ per double bond). If 0.105 g of a molecule of molar mass $304.5\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$ reacts with exactly 0.224 g of $\text{ICl}$, how many carbon-carbon double bonds are present in the molecule?
Butyl propanoate can be synthesised from 1-butanol and one other reactant. Compared to 1-butanol, the other reactant has:
options: more peaks in its $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR spectrum
the same molecular ion peak in its mass spectrum
questions.answer: The other reactant is propanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ ($M = 74.08$), and 1-butanol is $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{OH}$ ($M = 74.12$), so both have a molecular ion peak at $m/z = 74$ (D). Propanoic acid has more double bonds (C=O), a shorter chain and fewer $^{13}\text{C}$ environments (3 vs 4).

questions.question: 100 mL of 0.4 mol/L nitric acid, $\text{HNO}_3$, is added to 100 mL of 0.1 mol/L barium hydroxide, $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$. The pH of the resulting solution is
questions.answer: $n(\text{H}^+) = 0.4 \times 0.100 = 0.040$ mol; $n(\text{OH}^-) = 2 \times 0.1 \times 0.100 = 0.020$ mol. Excess $\text{H}^+ = 0.020$ mol in 0.200 L, so $[\text{H}^+] = 0.10$ M and pH $= 1.0$ (D).

questions.question:
The four substances below (butane, propanone, propanol and 1,2-ethanediol) have similar molar masses.

The substance with the highest boiling point is
questions.answer: 1,2-Ethanediol has two –OH groups per molecule, so it forms the most extensive hydrogen bonding between molecules and has the highest boiling point (D). Propanol has one –OH, propanone only dipole–dipole forces and butane only dispersion forces.

questions.question: Which one of the following would be classed as a weak, diprotic acid?
questions.answer: Carbonic acid can donate two protons and ionises only partially, so it is a weak diprotic acid (B). Sulfuric acid is strong, ethanoic acid is monoprotic and 1,2-ethanediol is not an acid.

questions.question:
The diagram below represents the distribution of kinetic energy in a sample of gaseous reactant molecules. The activation energy $E_{a1}$ has been changed to activation energy $E_{a2}$. This change increases the reaction rate.

Which of the following gives the most likely cause of the change from $E_{a1}$ to $E_{a2}$ and explains why the reaction rate would increase?
options: Catalyst added; molecules move faster, resulting in more successful collisions
Catalyst added; a greater proportion of reactants collide with sufficient energy to react
Temperature increased; a greater proportion of reactants collide with the correct orientation to react
Concentration of reactants increased; greater frequency of collisions, resulting in more successful collisions
questions.answer: Only a catalyst lowers the activation energy (the distribution curve is unchanged). With a lower $E_a$, a greater proportion of molecules have energy $\geq E_a$, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful (B). A catalyst does not make molecules move faster.

questions.question: The IUPAC systematic name for the following molecule is
questions.answer: The longest chain containing both groups has 4 carbons. The –OH group takes priority (suffix -ol) and gets the lowest number, C1; the $\text{–NH}_2$ is on C3 (prefix amino-): 3-aminobutan-1-ol (A).

questions.question:
A titration is performed in which a 20.00 mL aliquot of 0.10 mol/L hydrochloric acid solution is titrated with a 0.10 mol/L solution of sodium hydroxide. The pH of the solution in the conical flask is monitored and recorded throughout the titration.

Which of the following graphs shows the expected change in pH during the titration?
questions.answer: The acid is in the flask, so the pH starts low (pH 1 for 0.10 M HCl) and rises. Equivalence is at $V = \dfrac{0.10 \times 20.00}{0.10} = 20.00$ mL, with a steep jump around pH 7 for a strong acid/strong base titration (A). B is a weak acid curve, C has base in the flask and D has the wrong equivalence volume.

questions.question:
A student carried out an experiment, using the apparatus shown (a metal can containing 200 mL of water at an initial temperature of 22°C, heated by a spirit burner), to find the heat of combustion of ethanol.

1.80 g of ethanol was added to a spirit burner. When 1.50 g of ethanol was burnt, the temperature of the water increased to 48°C.

Calculate the energy released in kJ.
questions.answer: $q = mc\Delta T = 0.200 \times 4.18 \times 10^3 \times (48 - 22) = 21\,736\ \text{J} = 21.74\ \text{kJ}$ (A). The mass of water (200 g) is used, not the mass of ethanol.

questions.question:
50 mL of 0.10 mol/L barium hydroxide solution was titrated with a solution of hydrochloric acid and the electrical conductance measured as a function of volume of acid added. Graph A in the diagram was obtained (the titration was later repeated with sulfuric acid, giving Graph B).

Calculate the concentration of the HCl solution added.
questions.answer:
From Graph A the equivalence point (minimum conductance) is at 25 mL of HCl.

$\text{Ba(OH)}_2(aq) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaCl}_2(aq) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$

$n(\text{Ba(OH)}_2) = cV = 0.10 \times 0.050 = 0.0050$ mol

$n(\text{HCl}) = 2 \times 0.0050 = 0.010$ mol

$c(\text{HCl}) = \dfrac{n}{V} = \dfrac{0.010}{0.025} = 0.40\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$

questions.question:
50 mL of 0.10 mol/L barium hydroxide solution was titrated with a solution of hydrochloric acid and the electrical conductance measured as a function of volume of acid added. Graph A in the diagram was obtained (the titration was later repeated with sulfuric acid, giving Graph B).

Account for the shape of Graph A.
questions.answer: Barium hydroxide is a strong base and is fully dissociated into $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ and $\text{OH}^-$ ions, so the initial conductance is high. As HCl is added, $\text{H}^+$ ions react with $\text{OH}^-$ ions to form water, which barely conducts: $\text{H}^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O}$. The highly mobile $\text{OH}^-$ ions are replaced by less mobile $\text{Cl}^-$ ions, so the conductance falls steadily. At the equivalence point (25 mL) the conductance is at its minimum, but not zero, because the solution still contains $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ ions. After equivalence, excess HCl adds $\text{H}^+$ (very mobile) and $\text{Cl}^-$ ions, so the conductance rises steeply.

questions.question:
50 mL of 0.10 mol/L barium hydroxide solution was titrated with a solution of hydrochloric acid and the electrical conductance measured as a function of volume of acid added. Graph A in the diagram was obtained (the titration was later repeated with sulfuric acid, giving Graph B).

The titration was repeated using sulfuric acid instead of hydrochloric acid. Graph B was obtained. Account for the shape of Graph B.
questions.answer:
Initially the conductance is high because the strong base $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ is fully dissociated into $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ and $\text{OH}^-$ ions. As $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is added, two reactions remove ions from solution:

$\text{H}^+(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$ and $\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq) + \text{SO}_4^{\ 2-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s)$

Overall: $\text{Ba(OH)}_2(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$.

Since both the $\text{OH}^-$ and the $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ ions are removed (and the added ions do not stay in solution), the conductance falls more steeply than in Graph A. At the equivalence point (25 mL) all ions have been converted to the insoluble precipitate $\text{BaSO}_4$ and non-conducting water, so the conductance is (almost) zero. After the equivalence point, excess $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ ionises to give mobile $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{SO}_4^{\ 2-}$ ions, so the conductance rises again.

questions.question:
A buffer solution has the property of resisting changes in pH even when small amounts of acid or alkali are added to it.

Using equilibrium principles, compare the change in pH of a solution containing $\text{CaCl}_2/\text{HCl}$ in a 1:1 mole ratio and a solution containing $\text{NaH}_2\text{PO}_4/\text{Na}_2\text{HPO}_4$ in a 1:1 mole ratio when a small amount of acid is added to each mixture.
questions.answer:
Only the phosphate mixture acts as a buffer, so its pH changes very little, while the pH of the $\text{CaCl}_2/\text{HCl}$ mixture drops noticeably.

**$\text{CaCl}_2/\text{HCl}$:** HCl is a strong acid that ionises completely, $\text{HCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{O}^+ + \text{Cl}^-$, so no equilibrium is set up. Its conjugate base $\text{Cl}^-$ is an extremely weak base, weaker than water, so it does not accept protons. $\text{CaCl}_2$ is a neutral salt (from a strong acid and a strong base) and $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ do not react with water or with $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$. When acid is added, nothing removes the extra $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$, so $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ increases and the pH falls significantly.

**$\text{NaH}_2\text{PO}_4/\text{Na}_2\text{HPO}_4$:** this contains a weak acid, $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^{\ -}$, and its conjugate base, $\text{HPO}_4^{\ 2-}$, in similar amounts, in equilibrium:

$$\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^{\ -}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{HPO}_4^{\ 2-}(aq) + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$$

$\text{HPO}_4^{\ 2-}$ is a stronger base than water. When a small amount of acid is added, the increase in $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ shifts this equilibrium to the left (Le Chatelier's principle): $\text{HPO}_4^{\ 2-}$ reacts with the added $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ to form $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^{\ -}$, which is a weak acid and only partially ionises. Because there is a large reservoir of both $\text{HPO}_4^{\ 2-}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^{\ -}$, most of the added $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ is consumed and $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$, and therefore the pH, stays almost constant.

questions.question:
A buffer solution has the property of resisting changes in pH even when small amounts of acid or alkali are added to it.

A solution containing $\text{CaCl}_2/\text{HCl}$ (1:1 mole ratio) and a solution containing $\text{NaH}_2\text{PO}_4/\text{Na}_2\text{HPO}_4$ (1:1 mole ratio) behave differently when a small amount of acid is added: only the phosphate solution acts as a buffer. Provide reasons why the Arrhenius acid/base theory is inadequate in explaining the differences in behaviour of these substances.
questions.answer:
- The Arrhenius theory defines acids as substances that produce $\text{H}^+$ ions in water and bases as substances that produce $\text{OH}^-$ ions. It does not relate the strength of an acid (strong HCl vs weak $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^{\ -}$) to the position of an equilibrium when the acid is placed in water, so it cannot explain why one system establishes an equilibrium that can shift and the other cannot.
- It ignores the role of the solvent: it does not treat water as a proton acceptor/donor, so it cannot compare the strengths of $\text{Cl}^-$, $\text{HPO}_4^{\ 2-}$ and water as bases. It also cannot explain why $\text{HPO}_4^{\ 2-}$, which contains no $\text{OH}^-$, acts as a base, or the amphiprotic nature of $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^{\ -}$.

The Brønsted–Lowry theory (acids are proton donors, bases are proton acceptors, with conjugate acid–base pairs) is needed to explain the buffering behaviour.

questions.question:
Two students working together set up a simple game involving 40 separate paper clips. Student X was responsible for connecting individual paper clips into pairs, whilst student Y was responsible for taking apart the connected paper clips. Both students remained blindfolded during the game. After a while, the amount of individual and connected paper clips became constant.

State two ways in which this model relates to the essential features of a dynamic equilibrium reaction.
questions.answer:
- Both a forward and a reverse process occur at the same time: student X connecting clips represents the forward reaction and student Y separating them represents the reverse reaction. When the numbers become constant, the two processes continue at equal rates (dynamic, not static).
- The fixed set of 40 paper clips represents a closed system (no matter enters or leaves), and the constant numbers of individual and connected paper clips represent the constant equilibrium concentrations of reactants and products.

questions.question:
Two students working together set up a simple game involving 40 separate paper clips. Student X was responsible for connecting individual paper clips into pairs, whilst student Y was responsible for taking apart the connected paper clips. Both students remained blindfolded during the game. After a while, the amount of individual and connected paper clips became constant.

A third student added another pile of individual paper clips to the game. Students X and Y continued their actions. After a while, the amount of individual and connected paper clips became constant again.

By referring to the collision theory, explain how the addition of more paper clips to the game simulates the effect of concentration on a chemical equilibrium.
questions.answer:
Adding more individual paper clips models increasing the concentration of a reactant in an equilibrium system.

According to collision theory, a higher concentration of reactant particles increases the frequency of collisions between them, so the rate of the forward reaction increases. In the game, with more individual clips available, blindfolded student X finds clips to join more often, so connected pairs (products) are formed at a faster rate than student Y separates them; the equilibrium shifts towards products.

As more connected pairs form, there are more pairs for student Y to find, so the rate of the reverse reaction increases; at the same time the number of individual clips falls, so the forward rate decreases. Eventually the forward and reverse rates become equal again and a new equilibrium is established, with constant (but larger) numbers of both individual and connected clips. This mirrors Le Chatelier's principle: the system partially counteracts the added reactant by converting some of it into product.

questions.question:
The table shows some monoprotic acids.

| Name of acid | Formula | p$K_a$ |
|---|---|---|
| Chloroacetic acid | $\text{ClCH}_2\text{COOH}$ | 2.85 |
| Hydrofluoric acid | $\text{HF}$ | 3.17 |
| Cyanic acid | $\text{HOCN}$ | 3.46 |
| Formic acid | $\text{HCOOH}$ | 3.74 |
| Hypochlorous acid | $\text{HOCl}$ | 7.52 |

From the table, determine the weakest of these monoprotic acids.
questions.answer: Hypochlorous acid, $\text{HOCl}$: it has the highest p$K_a$ (7.52), i.e. the smallest $K_a$, so it ionises the least.

questions.question:
The table shows some monoprotic acids.

| Name of acid | Formula | p$K_a$ |
|---|---|---|
| Chloroacetic acid | $\text{ClCH}_2\text{COOH}$ | 2.85 |
| Hydrofluoric acid | $\text{HF}$ | 3.17 |
| Cyanic acid | $\text{HOCN}$ | 3.46 |
| Formic acid | $\text{HCOOH}$ | 3.74 |
| Hypochlorous acid | $\text{HOCl}$ | 7.52 |

Calculate the % ionisation for a 0.10 mol/L solution of hypochlorous acid, $\text{HOCl}$ (p$K_a$ = 7.52).
questions.answer:
$K_a = 10^{-7.52} = 3.02 \times 10^{-8}$

$\text{HOCl}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{OCl}^-(aq) + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$

| | $[\text{HOCl}]$ | $[\text{OCl}^-]$ | $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | 0.10 | 0 | 0 |
| C | $-x$ | $+x$ | $+x$ |
| E | $0.10 - x \approx 0.10$ | $x$ | $x$ |

Since $K_a$ is very small, $0.10 - x \approx 0.10$.

$K_a = \dfrac{x^2}{0.10} = 3.02 \times 10^{-8} \Rightarrow x = \sqrt{3.02 \times 10^{-9}} = 5.50 \times 10^{-5}$ M

% ionisation $= \dfrac{5.50 \times 10^{-5}}{0.10} \times 100\% = 0.055\%$

questions.question:
The table shows some monoprotic acids.

| Name of acid | Formula | p$K_a$ |
|---|---|---|
| Chloroacetic acid | $\text{ClCH}_2\text{COOH}$ | 2.85 |
| Hydrofluoric acid | $\text{HF}$ | 3.17 |
| Cyanic acid | $\text{HOCN}$ | 3.46 |
| Formic acid | $\text{HCOOH}$ | 3.74 |
| Hypochlorous acid | $\text{HOCl}$ | 7.52 |

A 0.10 mol/L solution of hypochlorous acid has $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = 5.50 \times 10^{-5}$ mol/L. Compare the pH of this solution to that of a 0.10 mol/L solution of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$.
questions.answer:
HOCl: $\text{pH} = -\log_{10}(5.50 \times 10^{-5}) = 4.26$

$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is a strong diprotic acid, so (assuming complete ionisation of both protons) $[\text{H}^+] = 2 \times 0.10 = 0.20$ M and $\text{pH} = -\log_{10}(0.20) = 0.70$.

At the same concentration the sulfuric acid solution has a much lower pH (0.70 vs 4.26), about $10^{3.6} \approx 3600$ times the $[\text{H}^+]$, because $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is a strong (and diprotic) acid while HOCl is a very weak acid that is only about 0.055% ionised.

questions.question:
A stage show requiring a frothing 'blood-like' liquid used dry ice ($\text{CO}_2(s)$) and iron complexes to produce this effect. One such iron complex consists of an alkaline solution containing iron(III) chloride and sodium thiocyanate. This produces the following equilibrium reaction:

$$\underset{\text{yellow}}{\text{Fe(OH)}^{2+}} + \text{SCN}^- \rightleftharpoons \underset{\text{bright red}}{\text{Fe(SCN)}^{2+}} + \text{OH}^-$$

The numerical value of $K$ at 25°C for this reaction was found to be $2.3 \times 10^{-4}$. What does the value of $K$ tell us about the equilibrium concentrations of the $\text{Fe(SCN)}^{2+}$ and $\text{OH}^-$ ions?
questions.answer: $K$ is very small, so the equilibrium lies to the left: at equilibrium the concentrations of the products, $\text{Fe(SCN)}^{2+}$ and $\text{OH}^-$, are very low compared with the reactants.

questions.question:
A stage show requiring a frothing 'blood-like' liquid used dry ice ($\text{CO}_2(s)$) and iron complexes to produce this effect. One such iron complex consists of an alkaline solution containing iron(III) chloride and sodium thiocyanate. This produces the following equilibrium reaction:

$$\underset{\text{yellow}}{\text{Fe(OH)}^{2+}} + \text{SCN}^- \rightleftharpoons \underset{\text{bright red}}{\text{Fe(SCN)}^{2+}} + \text{OH}^-$$

The numerical value of $K$ at 25°C for this reaction is $2.3 \times 10^{-4}$. Predict the colour of the equilibrium solution at 25°C.
questions.answer: Yellow (possibly yellow-orange), since the equilibrium lies to the left and yellow $\text{Fe(OH)}^{2+}$ predominates.

questions.question:
A stage show requiring a frothing 'blood-like' liquid used dry ice ($\text{CO}_2(s)$) and iron complexes to produce this effect. One such iron complex consists of an alkaline solution containing iron(III) chloride and sodium thiocyanate. This produces the following equilibrium reaction:

$$\underset{\text{yellow}}{\text{Fe(OH)}^{2+}} + \text{SCN}^- \rightleftharpoons \underset{\text{bright red}}{\text{Fe(SCN)}^{2+}} + \text{OH}^-$$

If dry ice is added to this solution, the pH changes from about pH 10 to pH 4. Explain why this pH change occurs.
questions.answer:
Carbon dioxide dissolves in water and reacts to form carbonic acid, which ionises to release $\text{H}^+$ (as $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$):

$\text{CO}_2(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3(aq) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+(aq) + \text{HCO}_3^{\ -}(aq)$

The $\text{H}^+$ ions first neutralise the $\text{OH}^-$ ions in the alkaline solution and then accumulate, so $[\text{H}^+]$ increases and $[\text{OH}^-]$ decreases, lowering the pH from about 10 to about 4. (The low temperature of the dry ice is not the cause.)

questions.question:
A stage show requiring a frothing 'blood-like' liquid used dry ice ($\text{CO}_2(s)$) and iron complexes to produce this effect. One such iron complex consists of an alkaline solution containing iron(III) chloride and sodium thiocyanate. This produces the following equilibrium reaction:

$$\underset{\text{yellow}}{\text{Fe(OH)}^{2+}} + \text{SCN}^- \rightleftharpoons \underset{\text{bright red}}{\text{Fe(SCN)}^{2+}} + \text{OH}^-$$

Adding dry ice to the solution lowers its pH from about 10 to about 4. Explain how the addition of dry ice produces the blood-red coloured liquid.
questions.answer: The carbonic acid formed from the dissolved $\text{CO}_2$ reacts with $\text{OH}^-$ ions ($\text{H}^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O}$), removing a product of the equilibrium. By Le Chatelier's principle, the system partially counteracts this by shifting the equilibrium to the right to replace the $\text{OH}^-$. This also produces more $\text{Fe(SCN)}^{2+}$ ions, which are bright red, so the liquid turns blood-red.

questions.question:
A solution of an unknown salt is analysed. It is known to contain either $\text{Mg}^{2+}$, $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ or $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ as the only cation, and either $\text{SO}_4^{\ 2-}$, $\text{Cl}^-$ or $\text{CO}_3^{\ 2-}$ as the only anion.

Outline a method that could be used to identify the cation and anion present in the unknown salt solution. Include relevant chemical equations and observations which would confirm the ions present.
questions.answer:
Use a fresh sample of the solution for each test.

**Anion**

1. Add dilute nitric acid. Effervescence of a colourless gas that turns limewater milky confirms carbonate:
   $\text{CO}_3^{\ 2-}(aq) + 2\text{H}^+(aq) \rightarrow \text{CO}_2(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$; $\text{CO}_2(g) + \text{Ca(OH)}_2(aq) \rightarrow \text{CaCO}_3(s) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$.
2. If there are no bubbles, acidify with dilute $\text{HNO}_3$ (to remove any carbonate) and add barium nitrate solution. A white precipitate confirms sulfate:
   $\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq) + \text{SO}_4^{\ 2-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s)$.
3. To another acidified sample add silver nitrate solution. A white precipitate that darkens in light (and dissolves in dilute ammonia) confirms chloride:
   $\text{Ag}^+(aq) + \text{Cl}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgCl}(s)$.

**Cation**

1. Note the colour: a blue solution indicates $\text{Cu}^{2+}$. Add sodium hydroxide solution: a blue precipitate confirms copper(II):
   $\text{Cu}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{Cu(OH)}_2(s)$.
2. Flame test (dip a clean nichrome wire into the solution and hold it in a blue Bunsen flame): brick-red flame confirms $\text{Ca}^{2+}$; blue-green flame confirms $\text{Cu}^{2+}$; no characteristic colour suggests $\text{Mg}^{2+}$.
3. To confirm $\text{Mg}^{2+}$, add dilute NaOH to a colourless sample that gave no flame colour: a white precipitate forms that does not dissolve in excess NaOH:
   $\text{Mg}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{Mg(OH)}_2(s)$.
   (Calcium can also be distinguished by adding dilute sulfuric acid or sodium sulfate: $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ gives a white precipitate of $\text{CaSO}_4$, while $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ gives no precipitate.)

Each ion must be confirmed by a positive test; it cannot be identified only by eliminating the others.

questions.question:
Compound X is a colourless liquid. When drops of sodium hydrogen carbonate solution were added to it, bubbles of colourless gas formed. When a few mL of X was refluxed with methanol and concentrated sulfuric acid, a product more volatile than X was formed. This product had a much more pleasant odour than X.

To what class of compound does X belong? Explain.
questions.answer:
X is a carboxylic acid (alkanoic acid).
- It reacts with the base $\text{NaHCO}_3$ to release carbon dioxide, a colourless gas (confirmed by turning limewater milky): $\text{RCOOH} + \text{NaHCO}_3 \rightarrow \text{RCOONa} + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2$. This is a test for an acid.
- Refluxing with an alcohol (methanol) and concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst is esterification. The ester produced has a pleasant, fruity odour and is more volatile (lower boiling point) than the acid because esters cannot hydrogen bond with each other.

questions.question:
Compound X is a colourless liquid. When drops of sodium hydrogen carbonate solution were added to it, bubbles of colourless gas formed. When a few mL of X was refluxed with methanol and concentrated sulfuric acid, a product more volatile than X was formed. This product had a much more pleasant odour than X.

0.62 g of X was mixed with 100 mL of water and titrated with sodium hydroxide solution using phenolphthalein as an indicator. 37.3 mL of 0.223 mol/L sodium hydroxide solution was needed to reach the end point. Assuming X is a monoprotic carboxylic acid, calculate the molecular weight of X.
questions.answer:
$\text{RCOOH}(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{RCOO}^-(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$ (1:1 ratio, monoprotic acid)

$n(\text{OH}^-) = cV = 0.223 \times 0.0373 = 8.318 \times 10^{-3}$ mol

$n(\text{X}) = n(\text{OH}^-) = 8.318 \times 10^{-3}$ mol

$M(\text{X}) = \dfrac{m}{n} = \dfrac{0.62}{8.318 \times 10^{-3}} = 74.5 \approx 75\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$

The molecular weight of X is about 75 (2 significant figures), consistent with propanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ ($M = 74.08$).

questions.question:
Nylon 6,6 is a condensation polymer formed from the reaction between hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioic acid in a 1:1 mole ratio.

Using condensed structural formulae, write the chemical equation for the polymerisation reaction.
questions.answer:
$$n\,\text{HOOC(CH}_2)_4\text{COOH} + n\,\text{H}_2\text{N(CH}_2)_6\text{NH}_2 \rightarrow \text{–[OC(CH}_2)_4\text{CONH(CH}_2)_6\text{NH]}_n\text{–} + 2n\,\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

Each repeating unit contains two amide links, so two molecules of water are eliminated per repeating unit (strictly $2n - 1$ for a chain with end groups). The paper's printed answer shows $n\,\text{H}_2\text{O}$; the correct number is $2n$ (or $2n - 1$).

questions.question:
Nylon 6,6 is a condensation polymer formed from the reaction between hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioic acid in a 1:1 mole ratio.

The molar masses of some species are shown in the table below.

| Species | Molar mass (g mol$^{-1}$) |
|---|---|
| hexane-1,6-diamine | 116.20 |
| hexanedioic acid | 146.14 |
| Nylon 6,6 | 244.31 |

If 220.0 g of hexanedioic acid and 280.0 g of hexane-1,6-diamine are reacted together in a vessel, what mass of nylon 6,6 is produced if the reaction goes to completion?
questions.answer:
$n(\text{hexanedioic acid}) = \dfrac{220.0}{146.14} = 1.5054$ mol

$n(\text{hexane-1,6-diamine}) = \dfrac{280.0}{116.20} = 2.4096$ mol

The reactants combine 1:1, so hexanedioic acid is the limiting reagent and 1.5054 mol of each monomer reacts, forming 1.5054 mol of repeating units.

Each repeating unit, $\text{–[OC(CH}_2)_4\text{CONH(CH}_2)_6\text{NH]–}$ ($\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{N}_2\text{O}_2$), is formed from one acid and one diamine with the loss of **two** water molecules: $M = 146.14 + 116.20 - 2(18.02) = 226.30\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$.

$m(\text{nylon}) = 1.5054 \times 226.30 = 340.7$ g

(Check by mass conservation: $220.0 + 1.5054 \times 116.20 - 2 \times 1.5054 \times 18.02 = 340.7$ g.)

Note: the paper's table value 244.31 corresponds to losing only one water per acid–diamine pair, and its answer $1.5054 \times 244.31 = 367.8$ g is therefore too high; the correct mass is about 341 g.

questions.question:
Nylon 6,6 is a condensation polymer formed from the reaction between hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioic acid in a 1:1 mole ratio.

Draw a segment of nylon 6,6 showing 3 amide linkages.
questions.answer:
A segment showing three amide ($\text{–CO–NH–}$) links, with alternating $\text{(CH}_2)_4$ (from the acid) and $\text{(CH}_2)_6$ (from the diamine) units:

$$\sim\text{CO(CH}_2)_4\text{CO–NH(CH}_2)_6\text{NH–CO(CH}_2)_4\text{CO–NH(CH}_2)_6\text{NH}\sim$$

Each C=O and N–H should be drawn in full in a structural formula (see diagram).

questions.question:
A laboratory assistant came across an unlabelled bottle containing an unknown white crystalline organic solid. The technician carried out several tests on the bottle's contents. The results (carbon-13 NMR, infrared spectrum, mass spectrum and proton NMR, with a table of $^1$H NMR chemical shift data) are shown.

Proton NMR data:

| Shift (ppm) | Splitting | Integration |
|---|---|---|
| 7.24 | 1 | 1 |
| 6.71 | 1 | 1 |
| 2.02 | 3 | 2 |
| 1.50 | 6 | 2 |
| 0.86 | 3 | 3 |

Draw and name the unknown compound that is consistent with all the information provided. Justify your answer with reference to the information provided.
questions.answer:
The compound is **butanamide**, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2$ (numbered C1 = carbonyl carbon to C4 = methyl carbon).

**Mass spectrum:** the molecular ion (parent) peak is at $m/z = 87$, so $M = 87\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$, matching $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{NO}$ (an odd molar mass suggests one N atom). The base peak is at $m/z = 59$ and there is a peak at $m/z = 44$ ($\text{CONH}_2^{\ +}$).

**Carbon-13 NMR:** 4 peaks, so 4 carbon environments. The peak at about 175 ppm is a carbonyl (C=O) carbon of an acid derivative (amide); the three peaks between about 10 and 40 ppm are $sp^3$ carbons of an alkyl chain.

**Infrared:** two strong peaks near 3350 and 3180 cm$^{-1}$ are N–H stretches of an $\text{–NH}_2$ group; the peak near 2960 cm$^{-1}$ is C–H; the strong peak near 1650 cm$^{-1}$ is the C=O stretch of an amide. There is no very broad O–H absorption (2500–3300 cm$^{-1}$), so it is not a carboxylic acid.

**Proton NMR:** 5 signals with integration 1:1:2:2:3 (9 H in total).
- 0.86 ppm, triplet, 3H: $\text{CH}_3$ (C4) next to a $\text{CH}_2$.
- 1.50 ppm, sextet, 2H: $\text{CH}_2$ (C3) with 5 neighbouring H ($\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2$).
- 2.02 ppm, triplet, 2H: $\text{CH}_2$ (C2) next to a $\text{CH}_2$; shifted downfield because it is adjacent to the C=O group.
- 6.71 and 7.24 ppm, singlets, 1H each: the two N–H protons of the amide $\text{–CONH}_2$ group (amide N–H 5–9 ppm), which are in slightly different environments.

All the data are consistent with butanamide.

questions.question:
A laboratory assistant came across an unlabelled bottle containing an unknown white crystalline organic solid. The technician carried out several tests on the bottle's contents. The results (carbon-13 NMR, infrared spectrum, mass spectrum and proton NMR, with a table of $^1$H NMR chemical shift data) are shown.

Proton NMR data:

| Shift (ppm) | Splitting | Integration |
|---|---|---|
| 7.24 | 1 | 1 |
| 6.71 | 1 | 1 |
| 2.02 | 3 | 2 |
| 1.50 | 6 | 2 |
| 0.86 | 3 | 3 |

For the mass spectrum shown:

(i) Identify the mass of the base peak.

(ii) Identify the structure of the fragment that produces the peak at $m/z = 44$.
questions.answer:
(i) The base peak (tallest peak, 100% relative intensity) is at $m/z = 59$.

(ii) $m/z = 44$ is the $[\text{CONH}_2]^+$ fragment, $[\text{O=C–NH}_2]^+$ ($12 + 16 + 14 + 2 = 44$), formed by breaking the C1–C2 bond of butanamide. The fragment must be shown with its positive charge.

questions.question: Draw structural formulae for both 2-methyl-2-pentanol (2-methylpentan-2-ol) and 3-methyl-2-pentanol (3-methylpentan-2-ol).
questions.answer:
**2-methylpentan-2-ol:** $\text{CH}_3\text{–C(OH)(CH}_3\text{)–CH}_2\text{–CH}_2\text{–CH}_3$. A five-carbon chain with both an –OH group and a $\text{–CH}_3$ group on C2 (a tertiary alcohol: the C bearing –OH is bonded to three other carbons).

**3-methylpentan-2-ol:** $\text{CH}_3\text{–CH(OH)–CH(CH}_3\text{)–CH}_2\text{–CH}_3$. A five-carbon chain with the –OH on C2 and a $\text{–CH}_3$ branch on C3 (a secondary alcohol).

In the structural formulae every C–H bond and the O–H bond should be drawn in full.

questions.question: 2-Methylpentan-2-ol and 3-methylpentan-2-ol are isomeric alcohols. Describe, and give the results of, a chemical test to distinguish between these two compounds.
questions.answer:
2-Methylpentan-2-ol is a **tertiary** alcohol and 3-methylpentan-2-ol is a **secondary** alcohol, so they can be distinguished by oxidation.

Test: place a few drops of each alcohol in separate test tubes, add a few mL of acidified potassium dichromate solution ($\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{\ 2-}/\text{H}^+$) and warm gently in a water bath (alternatively use acidified potassium permanganate, $\text{MnO}_4^{\ -}/\text{H}^+$).

Results:
- 3-methylpentan-2-ol (secondary) is oxidised to the ketone 3-methylpentan-2-one, so the orange dichromate solution turns green ($\text{Cr}^{3+}$) (or purple permanganate is decolourised).
- 2-methylpentan-2-ol (tertiary) has no H atom on the carbon bearing the –OH and is not oxidised, so the solution stays orange (or purple with permanganate).

questions.question:
The flowchart shows reactions involving eight different organic compounds A to H. Each compound (A to H) has a unique structure.

- Compound A ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_6$) reacts with $\text{H}_2$/Ni to give compound B ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_8$).
- Compound B reacts with $\text{Cl}_2$/UV to give compound C ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{Cl}$).
- Compound C reacts with NaOH to give compound D ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}$).
- Compound D reacts with $\text{MnO}_4^{\ -}/\text{H}^+$ to give compound E ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}$).
- Compound A reacts with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$/dil. $\text{H}^+$ to give compound F ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}$).
- Compound F reacts with $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{\ 2-}/\text{H}^+$ to give compound G ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_2$).
- Compound G reacts with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ to give compound H ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_5\text{O}_2\text{Na}$).

Draw the structures of compounds A to H.
questions.answer:
- A: propene, $\text{CH}_2\text{=CH–CH}_3$
- B: propane, $\text{CH}_3\text{–CH}_2\text{–CH}_3$
- C: 2-chloropropane, $\text{CH}_3\text{–CHCl–CH}_3$
- D: propan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{–CH(OH)–CH}_3$
- E: propanone, $\text{CH}_3\text{–CO–CH}_3$
- F: propan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{–CH}_2\text{–CH}_2\text{OH}$
- G: propanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{–CH}_2\text{–COOH}$
- H: sodium propanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{–CH}_2\text{–COO}^-\text{Na}^+$

G must be a carboxylic acid (two O atoms, reacts with carbonate), so F is the primary alcohol propan-1-ol. Since every compound is different, D must be the other isomer, propan-2-ol, so C is 2-chloropropane and E is the ketone propanone (one O atom). Note: in practice acid-catalysed hydration of propene gives mainly propan-2-ol (Markovnikov product), with propan-1-ol as the minor product; the flowchart requires the propan-1-ol product.

questions.question:
The flowchart shows reactions involving eight different organic compounds A to H. Each compound (A to H) has a unique structure.

- Compound A ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_6$) reacts with $\text{H}_2$/Ni to give compound B ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_8$).
- Compound B reacts with $\text{Cl}_2$/UV to give compound C ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{Cl}$).
- Compound C reacts with NaOH to give compound D ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}$).
- Compound D reacts with $\text{MnO}_4^{\ -}/\text{H}^+$ to give compound E ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}$).
- Compound A reacts with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$/dil. $\text{H}^+$ to give compound F ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}$).
- Compound F reacts with $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{\ 2-}/\text{H}^+$ to give compound G ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_2$).
- Compound G reacts with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ to give compound H ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_5\text{O}_2\text{Na}$).

Using the information provided, justify your identification of compounds D (propan-2-ol) and F (propan-1-ol).
questions.answer:
F ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}$) is oxidised by acidified dichromate to G, $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_2$, which has two oxygen atoms and reacts with sodium carbonate to form a salt, so G is a carboxylic acid (propanoic acid). Only a primary alcohol is oxidised to a carboxylic acid, so F is propan-1-ol.

D is also $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}$ but must be different from F, so it is propan-2-ol. Consistent with this, acidified permanganate oxidises D to E, $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}$, with only one oxygen atom: a ketone (propanone), which cannot be oxidised further. Only secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones.

questions.question:
The manganese content in a 13.5 g sample of steel was determined by measuring the absorbance of permanganate ($\text{MnO}_4^{\ -}$). The steel sample was dissolved in nitric acid and the $\text{Mn}^{2+}(aq)$ ions produced were oxidised to $\text{MnO}_4^{\ -}$ by periodate ions, $\text{IO}_4^{\ -}(aq)$, according to the following equation:

$$2\text{Mn}^{2+}(aq) + 5\text{IO}_4^{\ -}(aq) + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow 2\text{MnO}_4^{\ -}(aq) + 5\text{IO}_3^{\ -}(aq) + 6\text{H}^+(aq)$$

The resulting solution was made up to a volume of 250.00 mL. A 20.0 mL aliquot of the solution was diluted to 100.0 mL. The absorbance at 525 nm of the resulting solution was 0.50.

Calibration data:

| Concentration of $\text{MnO}_4^{\ -}$ (mg/L) | Absorbance |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0 |
| 10 | 0.2 |
| 20 | 0.4 |
| 30 | 0.6 |
| 40 | 0.8 |
| 50 | 1.0 |

Construct a calibration curve using the data.
questions.answer:
Plot absorbance (y-axis, 0 to 1.2) against concentration of $\text{MnO}_4^{\ -}$ in mg/L (x-axis, 0 to 50) on an even scale, with labelled axes including units and a title (e.g. "Calibration curve for absorbance of $\text{MnO}_4^{\ -}$ at 525 nm"). Plot the six points accurately and draw a straight line of best fit through the origin; the gradient is 0.02 absorbance units per mg/L.

Reading from the graph, an absorbance of 0.50 corresponds to a concentration of 25 mg/L.

questions.question:
The manganese content in a 13.5 g sample of steel was determined by measuring the absorbance of permanganate ($\text{MnO}_4^{\ -}$). The steel sample was dissolved in nitric acid and the $\text{Mn}^{2+}(aq)$ ions produced were oxidised to $\text{MnO}_4^{\ -}$ by periodate ions, $\text{IO}_4^{\ -}(aq)$, according to the following equation:

$$2\text{Mn}^{2+}(aq) + 5\text{IO}_4^{\ -}(aq) + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow 2\text{MnO}_4^{\ -}(aq) + 5\text{IO}_3^{\ -}(aq) + 6\text{H}^+(aq)$$

The resulting solution was made up to a volume of 250.00 mL. A 20.0 mL aliquot of the solution was diluted to 100.0 mL. The absorbance at 525 nm of the resulting solution was 0.50.

Calibration data:

| Concentration of $\text{MnO}_4^{\ -}$ (mg/L) | Absorbance |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0 |
| 10 | 0.2 |
| 20 | 0.4 |
| 30 | 0.6 |
| 40 | 0.8 |
| 50 | 1.0 |

Using a calibration curve drawn from these data, calculate the percentage by mass of manganese in the steel sample.
questions.answer:
From the calibration curve, $A = 0.50$ corresponds to $[\text{MnO}_4^{\ -}] = 25$ mg/L in the diluted solution.

The 20.0 mL aliquot was diluted to 100.0 mL (a factor of 5), so in the 250.00 mL solution: $[\text{MnO}_4^{\ -}] = 5 \times 25 = 125\ \text{mg L}^{-1} = 0.125\ \text{g L}^{-1}$.

$c(\text{MnO}_4^{\ -}) = \dfrac{0.125}{118.94} = 1.051 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$

$n(\text{MnO}_4^{\ -}) = 1.051 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.25000 = 2.627 \times 10^{-4}$ mol

$n(\text{Mn}) = n(\text{MnO}_4^{\ -}) = 2.627 \times 10^{-4}$ mol (2:2 ratio)

$m(\text{Mn}) = 2.627 \times 10^{-4} \times 54.94 = 0.01443$ g

$\%\,\text{Mn} = \dfrac{0.01443}{13.5} \times 100\% = 0.107\%$
